d: A leading, guiding; hence: mode of life, conduct.
me: Noun, Dative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means a person’s “self-conduct” or “way of life”—the manner in which someone lives and conducts himself or herself. It points to lived behavior as a recognizable pattern, not merely to one isolated action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Timothy 3:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is the observable way a person lives.

d: An Ethiopian, Abyssinian.
me: Noun, Genitive, Plural, Masculine, Location Gentilic
Noun, Nominative, Singular, Masculine, Location Gentilic

e.t: This word means “Ethiopian,” referring to a person from Ethiopia. It functions as a noun identifying an Ethiopian person or people rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both within Acts 8:27. The word itself identifies national or regional origin; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand the particular person or situation in which it appears.

d: Blamelessly.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: “Blamelessly” means living and acting without conduct that can rightly be charged against a person. It describes the manner in which someone behaves, emphasizing an upright life that others cannot fairly condemn. In the Greek New Testament, this word appears twice, both in 1 Thessalonians. Its first occurrence is in 1 Thessalonians 2:10, and its last is in 1 Thessalonians 5:23. The word focuses on observable conduct that is free from legitimate accusation, rather than claiming that a person never makes a mistake.

d: To find by seeking out, discover.
me: Verb, second Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Plural
Verb, second Aorist, Active, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to find.” It describes the act of discovering, locating, or coming upon someone or something. As a verb, it expresses finding rather than merely looking or searching. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 2:16 and Acts 21:4. The surrounding wording determines what is found and how the action fits the sentence, but the central idea remains the act of finding or locating.

d: To give up in despair, despair of; to hope to receive from or in return.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means to expect nothing in return; it can also express despair or the absence of hope. It describes a person’s inward expectation—or lack of expectation—when acting, giving, or looking toward an outcome. In its one New Testament occurrence, it functions as a precise word about having no expectation of repayment. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on receiving nothing back or on despair itself.

d: (literary and Jewish), without any preference (undue favor, partiality) for a person.

e.t: This word means “impartially”: it describes an action done without favoring one person over another. It functions as an adverb, telling how something is carried out rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Peter 1:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is fair, even-handed action.

d: A step (of a stairway); hence: a stage in a career, a position.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “standing,” referring to a person’s established place or status rather than an action. It is a noun: it names the condition of standing or the standing someone has. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 3:13. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence must be determined from that context; the core idea remains standing.

e.t: This word means “throwing” or “to throw.” It describes the action of moving or casting something away, whether by hand or into a particular place. As a verb, it can describe a deliberate act involving an object or person. The word appears 122 times in the Greek New Testament, so its precise force depends on what is being thrown and the surrounding sentence. Its central idea remains the act of throwing or casting.

d: A forceful, violent man; one who is eager in pursuit.
me: Noun, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word refers to a “forceful one” or “forceful person”—someone characterized by strength, intensity, or determined action. It is a noun describing a person rather than an action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 11:12. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea is a person marked by forcefulness or energetic determination.

d: To shed tears, weep.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to weep,” describing the act of shedding tears or expressing sorrow through crying. It functions as a verb, naming an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in John 11:35. The word itself identifies the act of weeping; the surrounding passage is needed to explain the particular circumstances and significance of that act in the verse.

d: To sail over (across).
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “to sail across,” describing movement by ship from one side or place to another. It refers to traveling across a body of water rather than simply remaining near shore. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:5, so its central meaning is clear but its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. The exact force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage and its description of the journey.

e.t: This word means to direct or command someone, expressing an instruction that guides what a person should do. It can describe giving an order, directing an action, or setting something in an arranged way. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 16 times, including passages where people are commanded, directed, or given instructions. Its central idea is authoritative guidance: one person or authority tells another what is required or arranged. The precise force in any verse depends on who gives the direction and what is being directed.

d: A test, trial, what is genuine.
me: Noun, Nominative, Singular, Neuter

e.t: This word means “testing”—the process by which something is examined or proved. It points to an examination that reveals whether something is genuine and able to endure. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in James 1:3 and 1 Peter 1:7. Its basic sense is the testing itself, while the surrounding verse explains what is being tested and what the testing produces or reveals.

d: A dragon or huge serpent; Satan.
me: Noun, Accusative, Plural, Feminine

e.t: This word means “dragon,” referring to a creature identified by that name. In the Greek New Testament, it appears thirteen times, all in Revelation, where it consistently identifies a dragon. Its use is therefore specific rather than a general word for any animal or person. The precise force of the word in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

d: To complete, bring to completion, carry out, perform.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, iNfinitive

e.t: This word means “to finish” or “to finish up”—to bring something to its intended completion. It describes the completion of a planned undertaking, emphasizing that the work reaches its endpoint rather than remaining incomplete. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Luke 14:29 and Luke 14:30. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

d: To work, trade, perform, do, practice, commit, acquire by labor.

e.t: This word means “to work” or “the one who works.” It describes carrying out an activity, laboring, or producing something through action. In the Greek New Testament, it is used 40 times, including descriptions of people working and references to God’s activity. Its exact force can range from ordinary labor to doing something purposeful, depending on the sentence. The word appears from Matthew through Revelation and commonly points to action rather than mere intention.

d: To run a straight course.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, first, Plural
Verb, Aorist, Active, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to sail straight,” describing direct movement by sea toward a destination. It functions as a verb for traveling in a vessel without following a winding or indirect course. Its meaning is precise and action-focused, emphasizing the direction and manner of sailing. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in Acts, so its recorded use is limited to this seafaring idea.

d: The Euphrates, boundary river of the province Syria.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: “Euphrates” is the name of a well-known river. In the Greek New Testament, this proper name identifies the Euphrates rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual virtue. It occurs twice, both times in Revelation, at Revelation 9:14 and Revelation 16:12. The word itself gives the river’s name; its particular significance in either passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

d: Esau, elder son of Isaac the patriarch, brother of Jacob.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Masculine, Location
Noun, Accusative, Singular, Masculine, Person
Noun, Nominative, Singular, Masculine, Person

e.t: Esau is the personal name of the man known in the Old Testament as Isaac’s son and Jacob’s brother. In the Greek New Testament, the word functions as a proper name rather than as a general description or ordinary vocabulary term. It appears three times, in Romans and Hebrews, each time referring to the same biblical person. Because it is a name, its basic meaning is identification: it points readers to Esau himself, while the surrounding passage determines what aspect of his story is being discussed.

d: Death-bringing, deadly.
me: Adjective, Genitive, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “deadly,” describing something that brings about death or has the power to cause it. It functions as a descriptive word, identifying the dangerous, life-ending character of something rather than naming the thing itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in James 3:8. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context, but its central sense remains clear: deadly or fatal.

d: Deity, Godhead.
me: Noun, Genitive, Singular, Feminine

e.t: Deity refers to what belongs to God or to the nature of being divine. It points to divine reality itself, not merely to a human resemblance to God or a religious title. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in Colossians 2:9, so its precise force there is understood from that passage’s surrounding wording. Its central meaning remains the reality of deity or Godhood.

d: Equal, equivalent, identical.
me: Adjective, Accusative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “equal,” describing people or things as having the same standing, value, measure, or comparison. It is used eight times in the Greek New Testament, including descriptions of equal treatment, equal status, or things regarded as matching one another. Its basic sense remains focused on likeness or parity rather than superiority or inferiority. The surrounding verse determines what is being compared, but the word itself identifies the comparison as equal.

d: And yet, although, indeed.
me: CONJunction or conjunctive particle

e.t: This word means “although” or “and yet/although.” It is a connecting word that introduces a contrast or concession: one statement remains true despite, or alongside, another statement that might seem to point in a different direction. It helps the reader notice that the following idea does not cancel the preceding one. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in John 4:2. Its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

d: To bear down, overpower; to give a vote or verdict, bring charges.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, first, Singular
Verb, Aorist, Passive, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine
Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine
Verb, Present, Passive, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This verb means “to cast against” or “to vote against,” expressing opposition to a person, proposal, or decision. It describes an act of taking a contrary position rather than supporting what is being considered. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in Acts, where its sense is connected with opposing or voting against someone. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on the act of opposition or the formal casting of a vote.

d: Weeping, lamentation, crying.
me: Noun, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: “Weeping” means the outward expression of grief or sorrow through tears or crying. This Greek New Testament word names the act or condition of weeping, rather than a person or a specific event. It occurs nine times in nine New Testament verses, appearing most often in Matthew, and is also found in Luke and Acts. Its precise force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the expression of sorrow.

d: Crippled, lame, especially in the hands.
me: Adjective, Accusative, Plural, Masculine
Adjective, Accusative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “crippled,” describing someone whose bodily movement or physical ability is seriously impaired. It is used as a descriptive word for a person or limb in the Greek New Testament. The word occurs four times, all in four verses, with three occurrences in Matthew and one in Mark. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a physical condition marked by significant impairment.

d: A hired servant, hireling.
me: Noun, Genitive, Plural, Masculine
Noun, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word refers to a hired worker—someone employed to work for wages rather than belonging to the household or group he serves. It describes a person whose service is connected with payment for labor. In the Greek New Testament, the word occurs three times: once in Mark and twice in John. Its basic meaning remains focused on the worker’s hired status, while the surrounding passage determines the specific situation being discussed.

d: A keeper-at-home, a housekeeper.
me: Adjective, Accusative, Plural, Feminine

e.t: This word describes being busy at home, giving attention to the responsibilities and activities connected with household life. It presents home-centered work as the basic idea rather than describing a particular occupation or task. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Titus 2:5, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central meaning remains clear: active, engaged, and useful within the home.

d: An unripe fig, one which, not ripening in due time, grows through the winter and falls off in the spring.

e.t: The word refers to a “late fig,” identifying a fig by its lateness. Its meaning is specific: it points to the fruit itself, not to an action, person, place, or abstract idea. In the Greek New Testament, it appears only once, at Revelation 6:13. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise significance there cannot be stated beyond this basic lexical meaning.

d: Always, at all times, ever.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “always”: it marks something as continually true, continually occurring, or consistently intended. It functions as an adverb, adding a time-related emphasis to an action, statement, or condition rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 41 times, showing regular use for expressing ongoing constancy across different contexts. Its precise force in any particular verse comes from the action or statement it modifies.

d: To form, mold, as a potter his clay.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Participle, Dative, Singular, Masculine
Verb, Aorist, Passive, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to form” or “to mold.” It describes the act of shaping something, like a maker giving material a particular form. As a verb, it focuses on the forming action rather than simply on the finished object. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Romans 9:20 and 1 Timothy 2:13. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains deliberate shaping or making.

d: To want more, need in addition.
me: Verb, Present, Middle, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “to need.” It describes lacking something necessary or being dependent on what is needed. As a verb, it expresses the condition of requiring help, provision, or some other necessity rather than having everything independently. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 17:25. Its precise force in that verse is determined by the surrounding sentence and passage.

d: A worshipper.
me: Noun, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “worshiper,” referring to a person who worships. It is a noun that identifies someone by their worship rather than naming the act or object of worship itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at John 4:23. Its central meaning is therefore straightforward: a worshiper is a person characterized by worship. The surrounding verse determines the specific emphasis in that occurrence, but the word itself names the worshiping person.

d: To sit with.
me: Verb, Present, middle or passive depoNent, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine
Verb, Present, middle or passive depoNent, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “to sit with.” It describes being seated together with someone or alongside others, expressing shared presence rather than merely movement toward a place. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Mark 14:54 and Acts 26:30. Its ordinary sense is straightforward: a person takes a seat in company with another person or group. The surrounding verse determines who is present and why they are together, but the word itself emphasizes sitting alongside others.

d: To meet, encounter, fall in with.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular
Verb, Aorist, Active, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine
Verb, Future, Active, Indicative, third, Singular
Verb, Future, Active, Participle, Accusative, Plural, Neuter

e.t: This word means “to meet”—to come face-to-face with someone or come together with them. It describes an encounter or meeting, rather than merely being near another person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times across Luke, Acts, and Hebrews. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on who is meeting whom and the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains a direct meeting or encounter.

d: To break in pieces, crush, thoroughly weaken.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “breaking” or “to break.” It describes the action of breaking something, expressing a forceful separation or damage rather than simply touching or moving it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 21:13. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and context, but its central meaning remains the act of breaking. d: A little child.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine
Noun, Accusative, Singular, Neuter
Noun, Vocative, Plural, Neuter

e.t: This word means “children” or “dear children,” and it can serve as an affectionate way of addressing those being taught or cared for. Its wording conveys closeness rather than merely identifying young people. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times: once in John and six times in 1 John. John’s letters use it repeatedly as a personal address, giving the word a warm, pastoral tone. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

d: To envy.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: To envy means to look on another person’s advantage or blessing with jealous discontent. It describes an inward attitude rather than simple awareness that someone else possesses or enjoys something good. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in Galatians 5:26. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains the desire or resentment expressed by envy.

d: Phrygia, an ethnic district in Asia Minor, the north-western part of which was in the Roman province Asia and the south-eastern part in the Roman province Galatia.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine, Location

e.t: Phrygia is the name of a region in the Greek New Testament. It functions as a place name, identifying where people were from, where they traveled, or where events occurred. The word appears three times in the Greek New Testament, all in Acts: Acts 2:10, Acts 16:6, and Acts 18:23. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s exact role differs by passage, but its basic meaning remains the geographic name Phrygia.
